item.title: Ten injured in knife attack at Polish school
item.description: Ten people were injured in a knife attack at a school in Ostroleka in northeastern Poland on Wednesday, a regional governor said, with police detaining the 19-year-old suspect, who was among those hurt, shortly after the incident.
item.dc:creator: Anna Wlodarczak-semczuk, Pawel Florkiewicz
item.content:encoded: Ten people were injured in a knife attack at a school in Ostroleka in northeastern Poland on Wednesday, a regional governor said, with police detaining the 19-year-old suspect, who was among those hurt, shortly after the incident. Masovian Regional Governor Mariusz Frankowski told reporters that nine people had been taken to hospital but that none of them was in a life-threatening condition. "The injured included five students, two teachers, and two bystanders, as well as the perpetrator, who inflicted self-harm," he said. Police said the suspect was a student at the school and that he had attacked people with a machete. They confirmed that bomb disposal experts were checking the attacker's backpack but were unable to say if anything had been found. STUDENTS BARRICADED THEMSELVES IN CLASSROOMS The attack took place at a vocational school for teenagers. Fire brigade spokesperson Adrian Stupski told state news channel TVP Info that students had barricaded themselves into classrooms in self-defence before they were evacuated. Authorities said the attack happened around 0900 GMT. Police said they detained the suspect about 20 minutes after the attack and posted a photo on X showing a man they appeared to have apprehended lying face down in a wooded area. Town hall spokesperson Katarzyna Ogniewska told reporters that all schools in Ostroleka were closed and that children were safe. The motives behind the attack were unclear. Such incidents are rare in Poland, but in September police detained a 13-year-old suspected of planning an attack and found a knife in his bag. (This story has been corrected to clarify that it was the regional governor who spoke, not Ostroleka mayor Pawel Niewiadomski, in paragraph 2.)

item.title: Aaron Sorkin on why he made another movie about Facebook, and how real life translates to film
item.description: Aaron Sorkin, the Oscar-winning screenwriter of "The Social Network," had been struggling to find an idea for a new project when he met Frances Haugen, a former Facebook employee and whistleblower.
item.dc:creator: Rollo Ross
item.content:encoded: Aaron Sorkin, the Oscar-winning screenwriter of "The Social Network," wasn't looking to make another movie about Facebook. Sorkin had been struggling to find an idea for a new project when he met [USN:L1N30T1LO TEXT:"Frances Haugen"], a former Facebook employee and whistleblower whose disclosures raised concerns about the impact on health, safety and global politics of the company's social media platforms. The story he crafted, told in the film "The Social Reckoning," will debut in theaters on Friday. "I was looking for a good story, and after a period of about a year of just epic writer's block, of not being able to come up with any story, I met Frances Haugen, and suddenly a good story started to take shape in my head," Sorkin, who also directed the movie, said in an interview with Reuters. "The Social Network," released in 2010, told the origin story of Facebook, which has since changed its name to Meta (META.O) , and starred Jesse Eisenberg as founder Mark Zuckerberg. The new movie centers on Haugen and journalist Jeff Horwitz , who wrote a series for the Wall Street Journal called "The Facebook Files" that began in 2021 and was based largely on thousands of internal documents that she provided to him. "It is a David and Goliath story, but there are two Davids," Sorkin said. "One is Frances. She picks up a rock and throws it at Facebook, and the other is print journalism. They pick up a rock and they throw it at tech." Horwitz, who later detailed the story in his 2023 book "Broken Code," now works as an investigative reporter for Reuters and remained on the Meta beat, earning a Pulitzer Prize in beat reporting this year with colleague Engen Tham for reports that exposed how Meta permitted its chatbots to engage in provocative behavior and earned billions of dollars in revenue from fraudulent ads. Sony Pictures (6758.T) bought the rights to his life story in connection to his previous Facebook reporting when employed by the Wall Street Journal. "The Social Reckoning" is a fictionalized account of events, and it does not draw upon Horwitz's reporting about Facebook, Instagram or Meta since he joined Reuters in 2025. The film chronicles Haugen's meetings with Horwitz starting in December 2020 and her reluctance to go public. Haugen eventually concludes the revelations will be more powerful with her name attached and decides to speak on the record. She also [USN:L1N2R02VT TEXT:"testifies before Congress"] to explain how she believed Facebook's algorithm was boosting divisive content in pursuit of profits. A Meta spokesperson declined to comment on the film. When Haugen testified, Facebook said [USN:L1N2R02VT TEXT:"the company disagreed with her characterization"] of how it operated. Zuckerberg defended the company in a Facebook post, writing that "the argument that we deliberately push content that makes people angry for profit is deeply illogical." In August, Meta [USN:L6N44N0VA TEXT:"agreed to pay up to $18 billion"] over the next decade to strictly limit how teenagers use Facebook and Instagram under a settlement with US states. The company denied wrongdoing and said ensuring that teens have a "safe and productive experience on our platforms" was an "absolute imperative" for the company. 'WHAT I DO IS A PAINTING' While Horwitz wasn't involved in the film's production and had no say over its content, he did meet with Sorkin and answered his questions about the reporting process and his relationship with Haugen. According to Horwitz, Sorkin said he would use some artistic license. "He told me that he thought he'd need to change some chronology and details to make the story he had in mind work," said Horwitz, who did not read the script until it was finished. "He also told me that he wanted to take some liberties with 'Movie Jeff,' who was sort of going to be a fictionalized, investigative reporter composite. It was definitely going to be an 'inspired by, not based on' situation." Sorkin said major facts of the story are accurate, although he had to create conversations and a timeline to make a compelling cinematic narrative. "People don't live their lives in a series of scenes that form a narrative by the end. People don't speak in dialogue. Those are things that screenwriters do," Sorkin said. "What you do as a journalist, that's a photograph," he added. "What I do is a painting." Zuckerberg, a supporting character in "The Social Reckoning," is played this time by "Succession" actor Jeremy Strong. Eisenberg declined the chance to reprise the role. "The Bear" star Jeremy Allen White portrays Horwitz, and Haugen is played by Mikey Madison, who won an Oscar for her role in "Anora."

item.title: Most Republicans in tight midterm races distance themselves from Trump, Reuters review finds
item.description: Reuters reviewed voting records, public statements and campaign materials.
item.dc:creator: Nathan Layne, David Morgan
item.content:encoded: Two-thirds of Republican candidates in competitive US House and Senate races have broken with President Donald Trump on policy or played down ties to him, a Reuters review found, revealing a widespread effort to distance themselves from the president as his unpopularity threatens the party's hold on Congress. The review of voting records, public statements and campaign materials found candidates in 41 of 62 competitive congressional races seeking some distance from Trump ahead of the November 3 midterm elections . The candidates have largely criticized or diverged from Trump on individual issues rather than repudiated his broader agenda. The findings suggest an effort to attract independent voters while avoiding a direct break with their party leader. Policy differences were the most common point of divergence, appearing in 23 of the 62 races. In 12 contests, the split centered on the Iran conflict, with vulnerable Republicans either voting to curb Trump's war powers or calling publicly for an end to the fighting that has raised gas prices and squeezed household budgets. Data centers are among the issues dividing Trump and some Republican candidates. Reuters identified three candidates in competitive races who have criticized or sought to slow such projects despite the president's support for faster development. The shift is notable because Trump has spent the past decade remaking the Republican Party in his own image and has been swift to punish lawmakers and candidates who defied him through primary challenges, personal attacks or public pressure to fall into line. In response to questions about the Reuters findings, White House spokesman Davis Ingle pointed to the administration's accomplishments and said Trump was "the unequivocal leader, best messenger and unmatched motivator" for the party. While news organizations have highlighted individual cases of distancing, the Reuters review is the first to systematically measure the trend across competitive races that will decide whether Republicans retain control of either or both chambers of Congress. A new [USN:L6N45R10Y TEXT:"Reuters/Ipsos poll"] underscored the challenge facing Republicans: Trump's approval rating remained stuck at a career-low 32%, while registered voters favored Democrats over Republicans 44% to 37% ahead of the midterms. Among independents, Democrats led 37% to 21%. CREATING DISTANCE FROM TRUMP Reuters also found a broad effort to play down ties: A dozen candidates removed his name, image or endorsements from campaign websites, most after securing their party's nomination. Others acted in subtler ways, skipping his events or declining to say whether he should campaign on their behalf. Direct criticism was relatively rare, underscoring Trump's dominance of the Republican Party and the risks candidates face in openly challenging a president who still commands the loyalty of many ardent supporters. Candidates distancing themselves from an unpopular president before an election is not unusual. Democrats employed similar tactics in the 2014 and 2022 elections. While Reuters did not conduct a comparable review of competitive races in the 2018 midterms during Trump's first term, analysts said Trump has rarely faced such widespread pushback by vulnerable Republican candidates. "(Candidates) are reflecting voter attitudes in these races," said Republican strategist Ron Bonjean. "If (voters) are not with Trump, then they need to show a break." Privately, campaign advisers told Reuters that candidates needed to dial back ties to Trump to attract independent voters. Publicly, they dismissed criticism of the repositioning. BALANCING ACT Republican Senator Pete Ricketts, who faces a tough challenge from independent Dan Osborn in Nebraska, exemplifies the 11 candidates identified by Reuters who broke with Trump on one policy issue while backing him on everything else. The balancing act was on display this week when Ricketts, who criticized Trump's plan to expand beef imports, joined the president at a Nebraska rally. "President Trump, I have been fighting for you in Washington," Ricketts told the crowd. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, a Republican in one of the country's most competitive House races in Iowa, has also shown a growing willingness to break with the administration. She was among 12 candidates identified by Reuters who split with Trump on multiple issues, criticizing his beef-import policy and later voting to limit his war powers in Iran after previously opposing similar measures. Yet, less than two weeks after her war-powers vote, Miller-Meeks joined Trump at the White House to announce a major steel plant investment in Iowa. "It is a balancing act," said Republican consultant Jeanette Hoffman, adding that candidates are trying to capitalize on the administration’s successes while creating some distance from Trump because of “how toxic the Trump brand is at the moment.” SCRUBBING TRUMP REFERENCES As Republicans in competitive races seek to expand their appeal beyond Trump's core supporters, some candidates have begun dialing back public displays of loyalty to the president. Mike Beltran, a former Florida state representative running against Democratic US Representative Kathy Castor, is among candidates who have scrubbed prominent references to Trump from their campaign websites. In August, his homepage featured a photo of Trump and said he stood with the president, according to the Wayback Machine, an internet archive website. Now Beltran's homepage shows only him and his family and makes no mention of Trump. Beltran's campaign had no immediate response to a Reuters request for comment. Representative Mike Lawler of New York, facing one of the most competitive US House races, embodies the balancing act confronting many Republicans in battleground districts: staying close to Trump while demonstrating independence from him. Lawler has highlighted breaks with Trump on issues including temporary legal protections for Haitian immigrants and a Trump-backed proposal to restore Turkey's access to F-35 fighter jets. His campaign manager Ciro Riccardi said Lawler acts on behalf of his constituency regardless of a president's stance. Lawler acknowledged the disagreements in a speech to Trump supporters at the Republican midterm convention in September, saying, "The truth is that the president and I don't always agree. And that's OK."

item.title: US consumer watchdog examiners adopt lighter touch amid pressure and threats, sources say
item.description: Examiners at the US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau gave a largely clean bill of health to most of the companies they inspected earlier this year, a light-touch approach that marked a departure from the past for the watchdog, according to three people with knowledge of the matter.
item.dc:creator: Douglas Gillison
item.content:encoded: Examiners at the US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau gave a largely clean bill of health to most of the companies they inspected earlier this year, a light-touch approach that marked a departure from the past for the watchdog, according to three people with knowledge of the matter. The CFPB resumed examinations in the spring after President Donald Trump's administration had suspended most of the agency's work upon taking office last year. More than half of those exams went through an "expedited review," which means supervisors identified at most only minor lapses with little risk of harm to consumers, making penalties unlikely, the people said. Such reviews are more lenient and were historically rare, said the people. But the agency's new political leadership had made it clear via policy changes and other communications that thorough scrutiny was unwelcome and that examiners' jobs were at risk, they added. The high proportion of expedited reviews, which Reuters is reporting for the first time, could expose consumers to harm if the agency overlooked or minimized serious problems, supervisory experts and former agency officials said. It also shows how the administration's effort [USN:S0N3VI038 TEXT:"to cut federal workers"], narrow exams, and encourage companies to report officials they feel are too tough on them is reshaping frontline oversight of the financial industry, they added. Representatives for the CFPB did not respond to requests for comment. The White House referred Reuters to the CFPB. SHIFT IN AGENCY FOCUS The Trump administration says financial industry oversight has become too onerous, hurting lending and the broader economy, though consumer advocates dispute that. It has also said it is trying to focus examiners on core risks. Russell Vought, the CFPB's former acting director, has accused the agency's staff of "thuggery" in their dealings with firms. He told lawmakers in July that it has shifted its supervisory approach with the aim of doing "as little damage as possible," adding: "That doesn't mean we're taking an approach to do... as little as possible." After initially vowing to [USN:S0N3TX02A TEXT:"abolish the CFPB"] — which Congress created in the wake of the 2007-2009 global financial crisis — the administration tried [USN:L6N40K10U TEXT:"to slash two thirds of its workforce"], including the vast majority of supervisory staff. Those plans [USN:L6N43C0UH TEXT:"are now on pause"] pending confirmation of a new CFPB director. The agency last year said it would cut the number of exams by half and refocus them away from what had been core areas, such as student loans and medical debt, and more toward mortgages and redress for military service members. It also said it would mostly focus exams on banks rather than nonbanks, such as payday lenders, which the CFPB alone oversees at the federal level. The agency also now requires examiners to recite [USN:L6N3WX14P TEXT:"a "humility pledge""] during exams to work efficiently, transparently and collaboratively with the company concerned. [USN:L6N43U16E TEXT:"Reuters reported in August"] that a top CFPB examiner reminded staff of that pledge and warned of "most unpleasant" consequences if they were too aggressive. Larry Lee, a former CFPB attorney who left the agency in August, said examiners have no incentive to look diligently for violations in the current climate, even as companies benefit long term from robust oversight. "Today's undiscovered compliance issues may fester and explode into tomorrow's widespread but preventable consumer injuries," said Lee, who now leads consumer financial protection policy at nonprofit Better Markets. EXAMS HELP CATCH PROBLEMS IN REAL TIME Under the rules, CFPB officials select for examination companies they believe pose the highest risks to consumers, usually after months of analysis. This year, roughly 70 companies were selected, about half the usual number, with examinations scheduled roughly evenly across four quarters, according to the people and a fourth person with knowledge of the matter. Reuters could not ascertain exactly how many firms were examined in the spring. Examiners typically inspect records and talk with company employees to uncover any compliance or regulatory violations before deciding how to proceed. In the past, most exams moved to a "full review," involving legal analysis of violations and internal discussions on whether the issue merits enforcement action. However, this spring examiners in most cases determined the inspections were "clean" under agency guidelines and proceeded with expedited reviews, the three people said. That means they determined that any violations were minor and unlikely to harm consumers, and it was therefore unnecessary to escalate them to legal or enforcement teams, according to public CFPB materials. Austin Hinkle, former senior counsel in the CFPB's Supervision Division, said that expedited reviews were traditionally rare because the process was designed to focus on the riskiest companies. "A significant number of expedited track reviews suggest to me that either political leadership simply picked the wrong companies to examine, or that when violations are identified, career staff are being told to back off," he said. Examinations are meant in part to correct problems as they are happening. In the past, examiners have identified and swiftly remedied improper vehicle repossessions, harassing or abusive phone calls, attempts to collect money that borrowers do not owe, overcharges and unjustified fees, according to CFPB materials. Lorelei Salas, who [USN:L1N3P20QG TEXT:"resigned last year"] as the CFPB's director of supervision after the agency halted the division's work, said she felt the CFPB leadership had demonized supervisory staff. She added that by no longer focusing on nonbanks, it was ignoring "companies that pose the highest risks to consumers" at a time when many are struggling. "The picture is pretty grim for consumers in the United States," she said.

item.title: Nobel chemistry prize goes to pair who solved mystery of 'mirror image' molecules
item.description: Scientists Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for solving a long-standing riddle of asymmetric "mirror image" molecules, a discovery hugely important for pharmaceutical manufacturing.
item.dc:creator: Marie Mannes, Simon Johnson, Johan Ahlander
item.content:encoded: Scientists Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for solving a long-standing riddle of asymmetric "mirror image" molecules, a discovery hugely important for pharmaceutical manufacturing, the award-giving body said on Wednesday. Soai, 76, is Japanese, and Kagan, 95, is French, and their work built on a discovery by the 19th-century French chemist Louis Pasteur. "This is the most exciting day in my life, I am very glad to share this prize with professor Henri Kagan," Soai said, speaking by phone to the Nobel Prize press conference, adding he had been out shopping when receiving the news. The Nobel committee was still trying to contact Kagan, the third-oldest person to be awarded a Nobel Prize, to inform him. French President Emmanuel Macron congratulated the laureates on X, calling it an immense honour for the country. "A recognition suited to a lifetime of research," he said. In fact, Kagan's work has long been seen as influential on the field and the then-French research minister complained to the Nobel Foundation in 2001 when Kagan was left out that year. The prize instead went to two American and one Japanese scientists for work in the same field. The chemistry Nobel, always the third prize to be awarded during Nobel week, followed those for [USN:L1N45R0AK TEXT:"medicine"] and [USN:L1N45S0E6 TEXT:"physics"] announced on Monday and Tuesday. 'RIGHT-HANDED' AND 'LEFT-HANDED' MOLECULES Many of the molecules essential to life exist in two forms that are mirror images of each other, like left and right hands. Yet living organisms almost exclusively use only one version, a phenomenon known as "homochirality" – from the Greek word for hand – that has puzzled chemists for more than a century. This year's prize was awarded for discoveries that showed how chemical reactions can be driven to favour a single molecular mirror image, work that has been key for chemists who design reactions for the manufacture of pharmaceuticals. "The left-handed version of the drug can have one effect, and the right-handed version can have another effect, and then we need methods for selectively preparing them," Peter Somfai, a member of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, said. "In developing such methods the findings of this year's laureates are important. They provided powerful tools for that," he said. BUILDING ON WORK BY LOUIS PASTEUR The first link in the chain in solving the problem was work by Pasteur, who died a few years before the Nobel Prizes [USN:L1N45N0AY TEXT:"were first awarded in 1901"]. He was looking at tartaric acid, important in the production of wine, and noticed that bacteria only ferment one of the two forms of tartaric acid – that which is naturally found in grapes. With the other there is no fermentation. That proved that some substances occur in two forms and that they have different properties, sometimes very damaging to health. How to create the right form of a chiral substance was a problem not solved until Kagan and Soai were able to produce asymmetric reactions, creating an excess of one form. The importance of the work is illustrated by the case of the thalidomide scandal in the early 1960s, when thousands of children were affected by birth defects caused by a sedative, thalidomide. When researchers analysed what had happened, they realised that it was the active substance's mirror image that caused the harm. PRIZES ESTABLISHED IN WILL OF SWEDISH INVENTOR Established in the will of Swedish inventor and businessman Alfred Nobel, the prizes for achievements in science, literature and peace have been awarded since 1901, with a few interruptions mostly due to the world wars. Nobel, a chemist by trade, amassed huge wealth in the 19th century from inventions primarily tied to warfare, most notably dynamite. The economics prize is a later addition funded by the Swedish central bank. Sometimes overshadowed by more famous laureates in the fields of physics, literature and peace, the chemistry awards have still recognised many influential discoveries such as nuclear fission and genetic sequencing techniques. Last year's chemistry award went to scientists [USN:L2N3VP07T TEXT:"Susumu Kitagawa, Richard Robson and Omar Yaghi"] for the development of so-called metal–organic frameworks, molecular constructions that can help tackle challenges such as climate change and lack of fresh water. The laureates will receive their medals from Sweden's King Carl XVI Gustaf at a ceremony in Stockholm on December 10, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel's death. The awards are followed by a lavish banquet at Stockholm City Hall. They also share 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 million), as well as the fame of winning arguably the world's most prestigious science award. The [USN:L6N44L0GC TEXT:"peace prize"], the only Nobel not presented in Sweden, is awarded separately in Oslo. ($1 = 10.0309 Swedish crowns)

item.title: Mayor of Turkey's secular stronghold Izmir joins Erdogan's party
item.description: The mayor of Izmir, Turkey's third-largest city and a bastion of its secular opposition, joined President Tayyip Erdogan's ruling AK Party (AKP) on Wednesday, amid a crackdown on the opposition in which dozens of mayors have been jailed.
item.dc:creator: Ece Toksabay, Huseyin Hayatsever
item.content:encoded: The mayor of Izmir, Turkey's third-largest city and a bastion of its secular opposition, joined President Tayyip Erdogan's ruling AK Party (AKP) on Wednesday, amid a crackdown on the opposition in which dozens of mayors have been jailed. Cemil Tugay, elected mayor in 2024 as a candidate of the opposition Republican People's Party (CHP) before quitting in June, formally joined the AKP at a ceremony in Ankara, handing Erdogan's party the mayoralty of a city it has never managed to win at the ballot box. "I have no doubt that, with harmony between the local administration and central government, we will achieve great things," Tugay said. The move is a significant symbolic gain for Erdogan's party in the western coastal city, long regarded as the heartland of Turkey's secular, social democratic opposition. The religiously and socially conservative AKP, founded by Erdogan in 2001, has never won the Izmir metropolitan municipality despite dominating national politics for more than two decades. Tugay won the March 2024 election with 49% of the vote, against 37% for the AKP candidate. The CHP also won 28 of Izmir's 30 district municipalities. MANY MAYORS ARE IN JAIL AWAITING TRIAL Erdogan's AKP suffered a major electoral blow in the March 2024 mayoral elections but since then Turkish authorities have launched an unprecedented crackdown on opposition municipalities that saw many mayors targeted with corruption charges that critics say are unfounded. Dozens of mayors, including Istanbul's Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu, who is seen as Erdogan's main rival, are in jail pending trial. Tunc Soyer, who was the Izmir mayor before Tugay, is also among those jailed as part of a corruption probe. The opposition has rejected the corruption accusations and says the investigations are politically motivated. The government says the judiciary is independent. Tugay resigned from the CHP in June after a [USN:L6N41Y0ZX TEXT:"court ruling"] that annulled the CHP 2023 congress and stripped Ozgur Ozel of his title as CHP chairman. However, he did not join [USN:L6N43Q11G TEXT:"the New Party"] founded by Ozel and 90 opposition MPs in protest over the court ruling and continued as an independent mayor. Ozel accused the AKP on Tuesday of using blackmail and the threat of imprisonment to pressure Tugay into defecting. "Those who refuse to bow to this pressure ... and do not betray their friends or their party will remain our brothers until the day we die. Those who sell out and leave are genuine traitors," Ozel told his party's parliamentary group. Erdogan rejected such accusations at Wednesday's ceremony. "Those who want to serve their cities in peace see the AK Party as the safest address," Erdogan said. "This is the reason for the growing support for the AK Party. Any suggestion otherwise is slander and speculation." Tugay is the second mayor of a large city to defect to the AKP from the CHP, after [USN:L8N3U60RK TEXT:"Ozlem Cercioglu"], mayor of Aydin, another western coastal city. [USN:L1N43N0LL TEXT:"Dozens of district mayors"] elected from opposition parties in 2024 have also joined the AKP since then.

item.title: Russia says plague institute worker's death does not risk an epidemic
item.description: Russia's health regulator said on Wednesday there were no risks of an epidemic breaking out in Siberia after a plague institute worker there died, as the World Health Organization pressed Moscow for more information about her cause of death.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Osborn, Jennifer Rigby
item.content:encoded: Russia's health regulator said on Wednesday there were no risks of an epidemic breaking out in Siberia after a [USN:L1N45S0CY TEXT:"plague institute worker"] there died, as the World Health Organization pressed Moscow for more information about her cause of death. Russian authorities say [USN:L1N45R0VI TEXT:"the 28-year-old laboratory worker"] died on Friday from pneumonia of an as-yet unestablished origin, in [USN:L1N45S0CY TEXT:"a case that has prompted international concern"], including from US President Donald Trump. Around 200 people were initially placed in quarantine. Global health officials - as well as the world's media - have been particularly alert to pneumonia cases of undetermined cause since the COVID-19 pandemic, which began with a cluster of fast-spreading fatal respiratory illness in China. However, the cause of individual pneumonia cases can often not be determined. The WHO estimates the risk of the Russia incident to the general public to be low based on currently available information. Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's health watchdog, said in a statement on Wednesday it was winding down precautionary measures it had put in place after concluding there was no risk of an epidemic and that it had shared its latest information with the WHO. [USN:L8N45S0R0 TEXT:"No cases of plague had been detected"] among anyone who had come into contact with the deceased worker, Darya Shipilova, it said, and 90% of those placed in quarantine had been released after nearly 5,000 lab tests had failed to detect any dangerous pathogens. It said Shipilova had been vaccinated and had therefore been "immune to the dangerous infections with which she worked". It did not say though what had caused the pneumonia which killed her or how she fell ill. WHO CALLS FOR MORE INFORMATION Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the director-general of the WHO in Geneva, said earlier on Wednesday that his organisation needed more information from Russia to understand what had happened. "WHO has requested further information to clarify the cause of the severe pneumonia, the pathogen that prompted the public health measures, and media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause," he said on X. "Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks." KREMLIN CRITICISES 'FALSE INFORMATION' IN MEDIA The Kremlin said Russia had properly informed the WHO about the incident in line with established procedures. When asked about the WHO's request to respond to reports about a second person in Siberia allegedly falling ill, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged caution when it came to using media reports as a reference for what was happening. "There is a great deal of media coverage, and the vast majority of what the media are reporting about this situation is false information," said Peskov. He advised the media and others to rely on information provided by the health regulator. It did not immediately respond to a Reuters comment request on Wednesday about the WHO's questions. EXACT CAUSE OF DEATH REMAINS UNKNOWN Some Western media outlets have reported — citing unnamed "Russian media" — that a second person in Siberia had died, saying they had died of plague. Reuters was unable to find any such stories in Russian media or any evidence that a second person in Siberia had died although some bloggers on social media were making — without evidence — such assertions. Contacted by Reuters, the WHO said it had nothing further to add on the matter beyond what Tedros — who was due to give a press conference later on Wednesday — had already posted on X. Tedros' call for more information echoed that of US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who has also said Moscow needs to share more information about the incident. Pneumonia, a lung infection, can have a variety of causes including plague as well as other bacterial infections or viral respiratory diseases, such as flu or COVID-19.

item.title: Australia prepare for first test in South Africa since 'Sandpapergate'
item.description: Australia play their first test in South Africa since the 2018 ball-tampering scandal when they start a three-match series in Durban on Friday, with the visitors unlikely to face more than a few heckles over the incident that rocked the sport eight years ago.
item.dc:creator: Mark Gleeson
item.content:encoded: Australia play their first test in South Africa since the 2018 ball-tampering scandal when they start a three-match series in Durban on Friday, with the visitors unlikely to face more than a few heckles over the incident that rocked the sport eight years ago. The tourists’ efforts to roughen up the ball using sandpaper, and aid reverse swing, in Cape Town in March 2018 were caught on camera and led to a major reckoning for the game in Australia, with captain Steve Smith among those banned for their role in the subterfuge. South Africa have played tests in Australia since ‘Sandpapergate’, and Australia have toured South Africa in the interim for limited-overs internationals. The scandal has attracted little media focus in South Africa over recent weeks in comparison to the attention devoted to the incident in the Australian press. After dethroning Australia last year in a thrilling World Test Championship final at Lord’s to win a first major title, South Africa are focused on improving their chances of a return to the final at the end of the 2025–27 WTC cycle. Australia are also in need of a boost after a surprise home test defeat by Bangladesh in August and with an Ashes tour to England starting next June. The pitch at Kingsmead often proves a fickle track but should offer the spinners a chance to play a leading role in a change from South Africa’s usually seamer-friendly surfaces. It is unusual for South Africa’s chances to be largely entrusted to their spin attack, but Simon Harmer and Keshav Maharaj wreaked havoc in India last November when they triumphed in their last two test outings. Spin was also a key factor for the home side as they beat Australia in the recent One-Day International series. South Africa may therefore opt to rest frontline attack bowler Kagiso Rabada from the test as he continues his comeback from a hamstring injury. Injury to Australia all-rounder Cameron Green opens up a chance at number five for Cooper Connolly, or a fairytale return for 34-year-old Nic Maddinson after recovering from cancer. South Africa’s also has a choice to make over their number three batsman, with coach Shukri Conrad having several options including a potential first cap for 30-year-old Marques Ackerman.

item.title: Gulf bourses retreat as Saudi-Houthi tensions surge
item.description: Most Gulf stock markets ended lower on Wednesday as fighting between Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces intensified on several fronts.
item.dc:creator: Ateeq Shariff
item.content:encoded: Most Gulf stock markets ended lower on Wednesday as fighting between Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces intensified on several fronts. Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces are [USN:L1N45T00S TEXT:"pushing a major offensive"] to retake ground lost to weeks of Houthi advances, backed by stepped-up Saudi air strikes. The Houthis [USN:L1N45T00S TEXT:"struck Aden International Airport"] on Wednesday with ballistic missiles and explosive drones, Yemen's Transport Ministry said, marking a sharp escalation in clashes with Saudi-backed government forces. Hostilities between the kingdom and the Houthis have escalated as well. Two attacks on Monday evening targeted airports in Jazan and Najran, injuring three people and causing limited damage, Saudi Arabia's aviation authority said. Saudi Arabia's benchmark index (.TASI) slipped 0.5%, dragged down by a 0.9% fall in Al Rajhi Bank (1120.SE) . The Saudi-led coalition, which is trying to retake strategic territory seized by the group, said it had [USN:S8N44F019 TEXT:"intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile"] fired towards Khamis Mushait in the kingdom's southwest. Meanwhile, there was no sign of a thaw between Washington and Tehran. On Tuesday, US President Donald Trump [USN:L1N45S12F TEXT:"said nobody knew who was running Iran"] during the conflict, which is now in its eighth month. Dubai's main share index (.DFMGI) fell 0.2%, hit by a 1.3% drop in top lender Emirates NBD (ENBD.DU) . Market sentiment remains anchored to geopolitical developments and diplomatic signals. While Qatar's mediation in US-Iran talks offers a constructive backdrop, the lack of clear progress continues to restrain risk appetite, particularly as disruptions to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz persist, said Ranim Turfa, head of research & market analysis, MENA, at Tickmill. Higher regional oil exports have offered some support, but the mood remains highly sensitive to diplomatic progress and any easing of shipping disruptions. Further escalation could weigh on markets, while meaningful negotiations and solid third-quarter earnings may help support a broader recovery, Turfa said. In Abu Dhabi, the index (.FTFADGI) lost 0.3%, while the Qatari index (.QSI) declined 0.5%. Outside the Gulf, Egypt's blue-chip index (.EGX30) eased 0.1%. Saudi Arabia (.TASI) fell 0.5% to 10,542 Abu Dhabi (.FTFADGI) dropped 0.3% to 9,960 Dubai (.DFMGI) eased 0.2% to 5,898 Qatar (.QSI) was down 0.5% to 9,210 Egypt (.EGX30) slipped 0.1% to 53,265 Bahrain (.BAX) lost 0.2% to 1,899 Oman (.MSX30) gained 0.5% to 7,828 Kuwait (.BKP) rose 0.2% to 9,064

item.title: Bulgaria halts rescue operation for crew of sunken ship
item.description: Bulgaria has halted its search for the missing crew of a ship that sank after being hit by a drone on Tuesday about 70 nautical miles (130 km) off its coast, Vice-Admiral Rumen Nikolov of the Maritime Administration Executive Agency told Nova TV on Wednesday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Bulgaria has halted its search for the missing crew of a ship that sank after being hit by a drone on Tuesday about 70 nautical miles (130 km) off its coast, Vice-Admiral Rumen Nikolov of the Maritime Administration Executive Agency told Nova TV on Wednesday. Early on Tuesday, [USN:L1N45S06O TEXT:"two ships"] were hit in a drone attack in Bulgaria's Black Sea exclusive economic zone. One sank and the other was damaged. The crew of the damaged ship were rescued, but the crew of the sunken one remain missing. Nikolov said the rescue operation for the crew of the sunken ship would not resume on Wednesday. "There are no traces of the sailors from the first ship, and there will be none. There is also no information about drone remains," he said on a Nova TV morning show. "A boat, three life rafts and parts of the ship's equipment have been found." It was not immediately clear who carried out the attack involving air and sea drones in waters off the coastal town of Byala in eastern Bulgaria, but there are growing concerns about [USN:L8N45R0NV TEXT:"hybrid attacks"] by Russia as it wages war in Ukraine . In an emailed statement to Reuters, the Russian embassy in Sofia said the merchant ship was not among the targets hit by Russian drones on Tuesday. Nikolov said the incident occurred in a so-called "responsible search and rescue zone" and not in the country's territorial waters, which extend to 12 nautical miles off the coast. In a separate incident, Romanian authorities said on Monday that [USN:L1N45R0CZ TEXT:"two people had died"] in a fire on a ship in the Black Sea outside the country's territorial waters. Bulgaria does not border either country, but as a NATO member it holds a strategic position on the Black Sea, where both Ukraine and Russia have major ports. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, speaking in a nightly video address, said an investigation jointly with Bulgaria's navy had shown that Russia was behind the attack. Radev said on Wednesday that following the attack his government would approve the purchase of five more surface-to-air missile systems.

item.title: South Korea unveils $747 billion energy transition plan through 2035
item.description: South Korea's government on Wednesday unveiled a 1,000 trillion won ($747 billion) energy transition and decarbonisation strategy through 2035, aiming to expand renewable power, transform heavy industry and create new drivers of growth.
item.dc:creator: Kyu-Seok Shim
item.content:encoded: South Korea's government on Wednesday unveiled a 1,000 trillion won ($747 billion) energy transition and decarbonisation strategy through 2035, aiming to expand renewable power, transform heavy industry and create new drivers of growth. The K-GX, or Korea-Green Transformation, plan includes 200 trillion won in fiscal spending, more than 790 trillion won in climate finance, alongside a separate 220 trillion won private-sector investment, Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il said in a presentation attended by senior officials and business leaders. President Lee Jae Myung called for South Korea to use its innovative edge to position itself at the forefront of the global green economy. "We must move away from the practice of chasing others and become architects and leaders of the green market ourselves," Lee said. The government is targeting 100 gigawatts of renewable energy capacity by 2030 and plans support for industries including green steel, batteries, solar power, wind energy, hydrogen and small modular reactors, according to a statement. It also aims for electric and hydrogen-powered vehicles to account for more than 70% of new vehicle sales by 2035 as part of a broader push to electrify transport and cut emissions. The strategy seeks to accelerate decarbonisation in South Korea's five highest-emitting industries - steel, petrochemicals, refining, cement, and semiconductors and displays - while fostering 10 green industries including electric vehicles, power semiconductors and carbon capture technologies. The government said it aimed to lead the global green steel market by becoming the first country to mass-produce hydrogen-reduced steel, while also supporting next-generation industries such as advanced batteries and SMRs. It also aims to commercialise tandem solar cells by 2028 and build domestic supply chains for key clean-energy technologies. Climate Ministry officials said the initiative was designed to address rising climate risks, energy security concerns and tightening global carbon regulations while turning carbon-neutrality efforts into a new source of economic growth. Officials also said projects receiving climate-finance support would be assessed for their greenhouse-gas reduction impact, while sector-specific decarbonisation roadmaps would be developed to help meet South Korea's 2035 emissions targets. SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won, who heads the private-sector consultative body supporting the initiative, said the K-GX strategy demonstrated the government's commitment to share investment risks with the private sector that had been hesitant to make long-term carbon-neutrality investments amid uncertainty over technology, markets and policy. ($1 = 1338.2 won)

item.title: IEA, EU discuss proposed oil, diesel stocks release, sources say
item.description: The International Energy Agency and European Union on Wednesday were discussing an oil and diesel stocks release proposed last week with diplomats and analysts expecting it to include volumes pledged in March.
item.dc:creator: Kate Abnett, Holger Hansen
item.content:encoded: The International Energy Agency and European Union on Wednesday were discussing an oil and diesel stocks release [USN:L6N45O0G5 TEXT:"proposed last week"] with diplomats and analysts expecting it to include volumes pledged in March. War with Iran and Ukraine has damaged refineries and disrupted tanker traffic, helping send diesel prices to record highs and impacting inflation and sectors including trucking and agriculture. Group of Seven countries [USN:L6N45O0G5 TEXT:"agreed on Friday"] to release 100 million barrels after President Donald Trump warned he might ban US diesel exports if they did not put more of the fuel into the market. It remains unclear how much diesel and how much crude oil will be released. On Wednesday, IEA countries met to discuss the plan, as did the EU's oil co-ordination group, diplomats said. The EU's energy task force was scheduled to hold a call at 1600 local time (1400 GMT), a European Commission spokesperson said. The G7 includes EU members France, Germany and Italy along with the US, UK, Japan and Canada. EXTENT OF NEW VOLUME NOT CLEAR The IEA advises industrialised countries and coordinates their emergency oil stocks for use during major supply disruptions. Polish Energy Minister Milosz Motyka said on Wednesday that Poland was ready to release oil and diesel stocks if a consensus is reached, but he did not expect an IEA decision on this on Wednesday. In March, the IEA announced a record [USN:L6N3ZZ01I TEXT:"release"] of 400 million barrels of oil from strategic stockpiles to combat a spike in crude prices and supply losses. Of this, about 325 million barrels have so far been released, the IEA said on Friday. EU countries expect the remaining 75 million barrels to count towards the new 100-million-barrel plan, two EU diplomats said. JP Morgan analysts also said much of the release in Friday's announcement would represent the completion of the March release. "Our interpretation of the press release is that the headline 100 million barrels does not represent 100 million barrels of new intervention," the bank said in a report. Germany's [USN:SPN45A00B TEXT:"economy ministry"] said it was working on the approval of the release of energy reserves without mentioning any new amount. "Germany will participate in the further release of the volume already determined by the IEA in March," the ministry said in a statement. (This story has been refiled to add the dropped word 'release' in paragraph 1.)

item.title: Pacific's new climate fund gets $15 million boost but remains far below target
item.description: Nations including Fiji and Ireland said on Wednesday they were donating about $15 million to a fund to finance climate resilience and adaptation projects in Pacific islands, but pledges remain far below the fund's target.
item.dc:creator: Peter Hobson
item.content:encoded: Nations including Fiji and Ireland said on Wednesday they were donating about $15 million to a fund to finance climate resilience and adaptation projects in Pacific islands, but pledges remain far below the fund's target. Pacific islands face acute risks from rising seas and volatile weather but say they struggle to access money from global funds. They are pushing for more donations at the pre-COP climate conference in Fiji. "This is the moment to invest," Mark Brown, prime minister of the Cook Islands, told delegates at the meeting. "Your investment buys us time." The Pacific Resilience Facility (PRF) is owned by island governments and aims to have $500 million after COP31, the UN's flagship forum for coordinating climate action, has wrapped up in November. It ultimately wants $1.5 billion. Pledges by Fiji, Ireland, the Netherlands and Denmark on Wednesday took its pot to slightly under $200 million, said PRF CEO Finau Soqo. Roughly half of that has come from Pacific island governments, New Zealand and Australia, according to the Pacific Islands Forum. "More is needed now," said Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. "Every investment now will make a difference and mean less cost of remediation tomorrow and in the future." Albanese was among representatives of 30 countries who on Tuesday visited the tiny atoll nation [USN:L4N45S08B TEXT:"of Tuvalu"], where they saw white sand dredged from the atoll lagoon to create new land that could withstand ever higher tides. The PRF aims to invest its capital and spend the earnings in what Soqo called a "small grants at scale" model. Its first two projects - restoration of a mangrove-fringed taro patch farmed by women in Palau and the restoration of a World War Two-era aquifer in the Federated States of Micronesia - were funded in recent months. It has since funded 12 more, she said on Wednesday. Over time, the PRF hopes to attract private investors alongside government donors, and eventually borrow money on international markets by issuing its own bonds, said Soqo, a former senior banker at ANZ, one of Australia's major banks. Asked if the PRF would reach its $500 million goal during this year's COP process, Fiji's climate minister Lynda Tabuya said she was optimistic. "This will be our take to COP31, and we hope our global leaders will come on board to support us."

item.title: South African rand extends earlier losses as dollar, oil prices climb
item.description: The South African rand extended its early losses on Wednesday, pressured by a stronger US dollar and higher oil prices, which dampened appetite for risk-sensitive assets.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The South African rand extended its early losses on Wednesday, pressured by a stronger US dollar and higher oil prices, which dampened appetite for risk-sensitive assets. At 1301 GMT the rand traded at 16.7025 against the dollar , down 1% from its previous close and 0.7% weaker than levels seen in the morning The US dollar last traded 0.5% stronger against a basket of currencies as investors awaited minutes of the Federal Reserve's September meeting for clues on future interest rate moves [USN:L1N45T02U TEXT:"Oil prices rose"], with Brent futures holding above $100 a barrel on continued Middle East supply risks and a storm heading for oil-producing regions in the US South Africa's central bank said on Tuesday the risk of second-round inflation effects had become [USN:L6N45S101 TEXT:"more pronounced"] as oil prices stayed higher for longer and El Nino clouded the outlook ETM Analytics said in a note that the rand has been about 3.5% weaker over the past month as high petroleum imports, especially diesel, created sustained dollar demand and increased the currency's sensitivity to oil prices On the Johannesburg Stock Exchange, the Top-40 index (.JTOPI) was last down 2%.
